Confidence
kon'fi-dens
n. (firm trust, boldness of reliance; rendering Hebrew kesel and mibtach, Greek parrhesia and pepoithesis)
From the Latin confidentia, from con and fido, to trust — a trusting-with, a leaning upon. Hebrew mibtach is from batach, to lean or throw oneself upon, and Greek parrhesia is literally all-speech, the freedom of a man who may say everything because he stands accepted.

Biblical Definition

Confidence in Scripture is always identified by its object, and the whole moral weight of the word lies there. Placed in God it is commanded and commended: “For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken” (Proverbs 3:26). Placed in men it is folly, and the Psalmist ranks the two without qualification: “It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man” (Psalm 118:8). Paul applies the same test to religious credentials, which are the hardest confidence to surrender because they look like godliness — the circumcision are those who “worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh” (Philippians 3:3) — and he then lists the pedigree he counted loss. The New Testament adds a second sense, boldness of access. Because the veil is rent, the believer may speak freely before God, and Hebrews urges him not to surrender that standing under pressure: “Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward” (Hebrews 10:35). Confidence in that sense is not self-assurance at all; it is the assurance of a man who knows whose blood brought him in.

Webster 1828 Definition

Firm trust, and also boldness of access. Scripture judges confidence entirely by its object — the LORD, or man, or the flesh — and urges the believer not to cast away the boldness Christ purchased.

expand to see more

CONFIDENCE, n. [L. confidentia, from confido; con and fido, to trust.] A trusting or reliance; an assurance of mind or firm belief in the integrity, stability or veracity of another.

2. Trust; reliance; applied to one's own powers or resources; self-reliance.

3. Boldness; courage to speak or act freely.

4. That in which trust is placed; ground of reliance; as, the Lord shall be thy confidence, Prov. 3.

5. In Scripture, no confidence in the flesh, Phil. 3; cast not away your confidence, Heb. 10.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 3:26 — "For the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken."

Psalm 118:8 — "It is better to trust in the LORD than to put confidence in man."

Philippians 3:3 — "For we are the circumcision, which worship God in the spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh."

Hebrews 10:35 — "Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward."

Modern Corruption

Confidence today means self-confidence — a quality to be built in oneself and projected. Scripture almost always treats confidence in oneself or in the flesh as the thing to be renounced, and locates true confidence outside the man.

expand to see more

Self-confidence is the modern virtue par excellence, taught to children as a foundation and to adults as a discipline. Scripture does not merely rank it lower; it names it as the rival. Philippians 3:3 defines the true circumcision partly by a negative — no confidence in the flesh — and the flesh Paul goes on to describe is not gross sin but an impeccable religious record. The most dangerous confidence a man can carry into the presence of God is the confidence that he has done rather well.

The correction is not that Christians should be diffident. Hebrews 10:35 commands the retention of confidence, and the same chapter has just described believers entering the holiest by the blood of Jesus. The principle to recover is the difference in ground. Self-confidence rests on an assessment of oneself and must therefore be maintained by favourable evidence; Christian confidence rests on the finished work of another and can survive an honest look in the mirror. That is why it can grow as self-knowledge deepens, where the other cannot.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew batach is to lean or throw oneself upon, giving mibtach, the object of trust; kesel is confidence and, in a bad sense, folly. Greek parrhesia is freedom of speech before God, and pepoithesis is settled reliance.

expand to see more

Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon, to feel safe; the root of the trust vocabulary.

Hebrew mibtach (H4009) — that in which one trusts; the object, not the feeling.

Hebrew kesel (H3689) — confidence; the same form can mean folly, a warning built into the word.

Greek parrhesia (G3954) — freedom of speech, boldness of access; from pas and rhesis, all-speech.

Greek pepoithesis (G4006) — confidence, settled reliance; from the perfect of peitho, to persuade.

Usage

"Of God as the object of trust: the LORD shall be thy confidence, and shall keep thy foot from being taken (Proverbs 3:26)."

"Of religious credentials renounced: have no confidence in the flesh (Philippians 3:3)."

"Of boldness of access not to be surrendered: cast not away therefore your confidence (Hebrews 10:35)."
